key_insight: Incidental, non-clinical information can leak into LLM-generated clinical notes and sometimes distort downstream reasoning, even when overall note quality changes only slightly.
clinical_relevance: Before using LLMs for ambient documentation or decision support, systems should be tested for resistance to irrelevant speech, small talk, and other bystander information that can contaminate outputs.
method: Evaluated 576 patient-clinician dialogues for small-talk contamination in generated notes
Tested 57 mock recorded consultations with background speech at -10 dB to assess transcript and note contamination
Compared frontier models and four open-weight models using note quality and contamination metrics
evidence_signal: Frontier models inserted small-talk into 35% of notes, with 3.7% showing misattribution or clinical use of asides; background speech leaked into 48.2% of transcripts and into 5.3% of downstream notes.
watch_item: The study shows contamination can occur even when average quality scores remain stable, so deployment safeguards must detect incidental-information leakage without suppressing clinically relevant content.
paper_title: Incidental information contaminates patient notes and disrupts clinical reasoning in large language models
